paper_title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in single set of weights and are widely seen as route to general-purpose intelligence. However, the lack of interpretability of models internal working mechanism (Zhao et al., 2024), and the controversy on whether it has genuine reasoning capability rather than pattern matching (Mirzadeh et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024), make that route questionable (Dawid and LeCun, 2024), especially in high-stakes scenarios such as healthcare. Neuro-symbolic models (dAvila Garcez and Lamb, 2023; Kautz, 2022), instead, address the two defects of LLMs architecturally: symbolic component exposes intermediate states that person can read and intervene on (Yang, 2026), and supplies the slow, deliberate, and usually rule-governed reasoning capability that cognitive theory calls System 2 (Kahneman, 2011; Booch et al., 2021; Goyal and Bengio, 2022). Yet major challenge that blocks neurosymbolic models is scalability. Unlike LLMs whose knowledge is obtained via self-supervised learning on an enormous corpus, which benefits from modern computing hardware, symbolic systems depend on knowledge and careful handcraft from human experts. Consequently, most existing symbolic systems and neuro-symbolic models are confined to one domain (The mathlib Community, 2020; Ashburner et al., 2000; Silver et al., 2016; Segler et al., 2018; Lample and Charton, 2020). Nonetheless, much symbolic knowledge does already exist, and AI now adds to it, e.g., Lean proofs on open problems (OpenAI, 2026). But it is spread across those numerous domain-specific systems that each describe it in their own schema: math problem is Lean 4 theorem in one proof assistant and string of $e hypotheses in Metamath, and the same place is TrainStation in one knowledge graph and RailwayStation in another. Indeed, aligning such heterogeneous systems is classic problem in several communitiesontology matching (Euzenat and Shvaiko, 2013), schema matching (Rahm and Bernstein, 2001), entity alignment (Sun et al., 2020), cross-language code retrieval (Zhu et al., 2022)but each solves it for its own kind of system. We use one term, symbolic matching, for all of them, and general approach to it is the first step towards the universal symbolic backbone that general-purpose neuro-symbolic model needs, reusing the human effort in existing systems instead of starting over like Cyc (Lenat, Figure 1: SAE-IDF on the NELL class trainstation (Common-KG NELL DBpedia). (3) Its largest coordinates, with explanations and document frequencies: idf damps features that fire on many symbols (grey). (4) Each bar is features share of the cosine with the query; the mark says whether it is the gold: 93% of the match with the gold RailwayStation comes from two features for railroads and stations, whereas dense ranks the gold fifth and AutombileEngine (sic) first, which shares only ubiquitous or unrelated features and ranks fourth under SAE-IDF. 1995). One might think pretrained LLM already supplies general tool for symbolic matching: trained on large general corpus, it reads almost any notation and contextualizes each symbol through attention (Vaswani et al., 2017). Its hidden states are natural candidate, but they are known to be anisotropic, dominated by directions shared by all inputs (Ethayarajh, 2019; Mu and Viswanath, 2018), and dense text embeddings tend to favor superficial linguistic similarity over structural correspondence (Yang et al., 2024). Neither defect is easy to fix: each dense dimension mixes many concepts in superposition (Elhage et al., 2022), so it can be neither rarity-weighted nor read to explain match, and post-hoc fixes such as whitening trail SAE-IDF on most tasks (Appendix K). Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) address these defects. They write an LLMs hidden state as sparse sum of interpretable features from large dictionary (Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024). Trained on large corpus, the dictionary is shared coordinate system for any token, including symbols: each feature is basis direction and its weight (the code) the coordinate. Here, the directions shared by every dense vector become few named, ubiquitous features that can be identified and downweighted, as well as lexical features, so each symbols contextual meaning contributes most to the matching. Upon such merits, we build SAE-IDF, general approach for symbolic matching. An LLM reads each symbol in its native context; the SAE encodes it as sparse code, in effect bag of named concepts, so text retrievals classic inverse document frequency (IDF; Spärck Jones, 1972) applies: features are weighted by rarity and candidates ranked by the cosine of weighted codes (Figure 1), much as DNA sequence search finds relatedness in few high-scoring local matches, each scored against chance (Altschul et al., 1990), not in stretches every genome shares. Needing no aligned pairs, SAE-IDF matches any systems an LLM can read. Across 12 tasks on 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF beats the same models dense hidden state on every task with Gemma-2-9B and on all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, and it is the best trainingfree method on most tasks. Our main contributions are as follows: SAE-IDF, training-free, general and interpretable approach to symbolic matching that significantly outperforms baselines (Sections 2, 3). Ablations showing that both ingredients matter and the gain is robust (Sections 4.1, 4.2). feature-level interpretability analysis with ruleselected case studies, column-type split and merge tests (Sections 4.3, 5).

sections.title: 3.1 Datasets
sections.content: Six different kinds of symbolic systems were chosen to test the universal applicability of SAE-IDF, where every run uses the full test data and the benchmarks own metric code where one exists. miniF2F (Zheng et al., 2022): from the Lean 4 port (Yang, 2023) we retrieve each problems statement in another prover among all statements of that prover, with names, proofs, comments and labels stripped so that nothing but the mathematics identifies problem. XLCoST (Zhu et al., 2022): the official protocol and evaluator (the pool contains the querys own row, free first hit); MRR and Precision@6 averaged over the seven query languages. Valentine (Koutras et al., 2021): all 551 joinable and unionable pairs, scored with Valentines F1 (one-to-one assignment) and MRR. Common-KG (Fallatah et al., 2020): 129 NELLDBpedia reference pairs and 304 YAGOWikidata pairs; classes without instances match on their label alone. MultiFarm (Meilicke et al., 2012): foreign-language terms against the English terms of different conference ontology, so that neither language nor ontology is shared. Bio-ML (He et al., 2022b) and OAEI Anatomy (Bodenreider et al., 2005): biomedical ontologies, NCIT DOID on the Bio-ML validation split with its 100-candidate ranking protocol, and mouse human anatomy against all 3,298 human classes; about half of their gold pairs have identical labels. The metric is MRR unless stated; Appendix gives view formats. PubChem SMILES / IUPAC / InChI (Kim et al., 2023), notations the model cannot read, are in Appendix D.

The empirical result confirms the benefit of scaling up in symbolic matching tasks: for example, HOL Light MRR rises from 0.87 to 0.94 and Metamath from 0.65 to 0.74 across Gemma-2-2B, 9B and 27B (Section 4.2), whereas retriever is bounded by its training pairs and must be retrained at each size. retriever must also be trained on aligned pairs from the domain it will serve, which newly encountered pair of systems does not have; SAE-IDF needs none, which is why one method covers all six kinds of system here.

Across all 39 configurations, including different SAE layers, SAE width, sparsity levels and model families and sizes, SAE-IDF consistently beats both dense and DensePC1 on both tasks, by +0.18 to +0.55 MRR over dense on HOL Light and +0.08 to +0.58 on Metamath, and beats SAE-unweighted in all 78 runs, by +0.11 to +0.66. At nearly fixed sparsity, SAE-IDF rises with every doubling of the dictionary on HOL Light (0.817 at 16k to 0.935 at 1M) and levels off from 65k on Metamath, while SAE-unweighted drifts down as it widens. The same sweeps on Common-KG and MultiFarm agree (Figure 5). The effect holds from 2B to 27B parameters (Gemma-2-27B: 0.939 and 0.738 vs. dense 0.41 and 0.20) and for second model family: with Llama-3.1-8B and Llama Scope, SAE-IDF beats dense in all six miniF2F configurations  (Table 14)  .

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Optimal choice between neural and symbolic representations. neuro-symbolic system must decide which knowledge to leave to its symbolic component (Yang, 2026). Rules are exact where identity is fixed by definition (equal keys, units, formats), while neural representations suit graded similarity, the family resemblance of Wittgenstein (1953). Splitting the 551 Valentine pairs by the kind of value column holds (Appendix C), SAE-IDF leads dense in every class, with top-1 accuracy of 0.790.81 on free-text, categorical and identifier columns but 0.67 on numeric ones, the hardest class for every method. This indicates that bare numbers, which give the features the least to match, are where rules on ranges, units and value distributions should take over, hypothesis for future work. Merging many systems needs pairwise alignments that agree (A to then to equals to C) and links that group symbols by their true identity. Over the twelve ordered pairs among the four provers, with mutual top-1 matches as links, SAE-IDF links almost twice as many statements as dense (coverage 0.64 vs. 0.34) at equal or higher consistency (transitivity 0.981 vs. 0.963; purity 0.981 vs. 0.979), and its merge comes closest to the true grouping (adjusted Rand index 0.795; dense 0.519, DensePC1 0.646; Table 4, Appendix H). shared space alone does not ensure this: the unweighted code, in the same space, is the least consistent (transitivity 0.902, purity 0.958). merge also needs abstention, since under transitive closure one false link fuses two correct clusters. For answering selectively, the cosine margin between the first two candidates is usable confidence: at 90% precision SAE-IDF answers 24% of Metamath and 93% of HOL Light queries, against 1% and 24% for dense (Appendix J).

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Alignment within one kind of system. Ontology matching has yearly evaluation (OAEI) and many systems, from logic-based lexical matchers such as LogMap (Jiménez-Ruiz and Cuenca Grau, 2011) to fine-tuned language models (He et al., 2022a), prompted LLMs (Hertling and Paulheim, 2023) and LLM agents (Qiang et al., 2024); Euzenat and Shvaiko (2013) survey it. Schema matching (Rahm and Bernstein, 2001; Koutras et al., 2021), entity alignment from seed pairs (Sun et al., 2020) and cross-language code retrieval (Feng et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2022) each have their own methods and benchmarks; none runs unchanged on another kind of system (Section 3.2). Sparse autoencoders. SAEs recover sparse, interpretable features from superposed activations (Elhage et al., 2022; Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025), are released as open suites (Lieberum et al., 2024; He et al., 2024), and give interpretable axes for semantic search when trained on text embeddings (ONeill et al., 2024). Against doubts about their downstream use (Kantamneni et al., 2025), they help here once the code is rarity-weighted. Neuro-symbolic models. Neuro-symbolic systems combine learned representations with explicit symbolic structure (Kautz, 2022): differentiable logic and proving (Logic Tensor Networks, Badreddine et al., 2022; neural theorem provers, Rocktäschel and Riedel, 2017; NLProlog, Weber et al., 2019; ILP, Evans and Grefenstette, 2018), probabilistic logic programs over neural predicates (DeepProbLog, Manhaeve et al., 2018), symbolic programs run over neural scene parses (NS-CL, Mao et al., 2019), and language models paired with symbolic solvers or deduction engines (LogicLM, Pan et al., 2023; AlphaGeometry, Trinh et al., 2024). Each reasons inside formalisms chosen for its task; none aligns the symbols of independently built systems, the step universal symbolic backbone needs (Yang, 2026) and the one we address.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: SAE-IDF matches symbols across heterogeneous systems without training: native context, an LLMs sparse autoencoder, rarity weighting and cosine. On 12 tasks across six kinds of system it beats the same models dense state on every task with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B; both the dictionary and the weighting are needed, and each match reads as few rare, named concepts. An LLMs feature dictionary is thus an interpretable common ground for aligning symbolic systems, step toward universal backbone.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: What the model can read. The method is only as general as the base models reading of each notation and the native context each system offers: it is at chance on SMILES, IUPAC names and InChI, on par with word TF-IDF when two notations share their identifiers (XLCoST), short of context on MultiFarm, Anatomy and label-only knowledge-graph classes, and we dropped context-less symbols such as ICD codes and drug names. Protocol. Every task ranks given candidate pool in which the query has counterpart, with one layer per model. real merging pipeline must also decide how many counterparts symbol hasnone, one or several under the structural constraints of the merged systems, and be tested by merging many systems with transitivity as the criterion; our margin-based abstention covers only queries that have counterpart, and such full alignments are left to future work. Comparisons. We compare representations, not dedicated pipelines, and claim no state of the art on any benchmark. Trained retrievers lead on formal mathematics, where memorized aligned statements are possible; the lead over DensePC1 is within noise on MultiFarm and NELL DBpedia and smaller with Llama-3.1-8B; and the idf is computed on the pool being matched (Appendix tests held-out library). Explanations. Feature names are generated automatically and their types labelled by an LLM; they describe matches but never compute them.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Artifacts and licenses. We use released models, SAEs and benchmarks for research inference and evaluation only, with no fine-tuning and no redistribution of weights or data, which is consistent with their terms: Gemma 2 under the Gemma Terms of Use and its Prohibited Use Policy, which also cover Gemma Scope (released under CC BY 4.0); Llama-3.1-8B under the Llama 3.1 Community License and its Acceptable Use Policy; Llama Scope and Qwen3-Embedding-8B under Apache2.0; BGE-M3 under MIT. miniF2F is released under Apache-2.0 (Lean, Isabelle), MIT (Metamath) and FreeBSD (HOL Light) licenses, miniF2F-lean4 under MIT, Bio-ML and the two Anatomy ontologies (MA, NCI Thesaurus) under CC BY 4.0; MultiFarm may be used for any scientific purpose and NCBI places no restrictions on PubChem data; XLCoST, Valentine, the OAEI Common-KG track and the Neuronpedia feature explanations are distributed by their authors for research and evaluation without stated data license. Every artifact is cited. Data. The tasks consist of formal statements, programs, table schemas with sampled cell values from the public benchmark tables, and ontology and knowledge-graph terms; we collected no data from people and add no personal information. Risks. Automatic matching can propagate errors: under transitive closure one false link fuses two correct clusters (Section 5), so merges built on SAE-IDF should use abstention or human review, especially for high-stakes resources such as biomedical ontologies. Feature names are generated automatically and can mislead reader about why match was made.

The main-table SAE is layer_20/width_131k/average_l0_114, the canonical release, which is the one with Neuronpedia explanations. Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers, = 4,096) uses the Llama Scope residual SAEs Llama3_1-8B-Base-L{8,12,15,20,24}R-32x (131k features) and L15R-8x (32k), applied as published, with dataset-wise input scaling and the released JumpReLU threshold. Texts are truncated to 1,024 tokens (15 of 3,918 Java programs were truncated). released Class: Views. Common-KG: up to 16 instances per class sampled with fixed seed, written Instance: <label>; class with no <label>. instances gets the single view Class: <label>. MultiFarm: one view per axiom of the term in its own ontology and language (parents and children, domain and range, properties whose domain or range it is, suband super-properties, inverses, disjoint classes), written <relation> <other>. Term: <label>. Bio-ML and Anatomy: definitions, parents and part-of relations in the same form. Valentine: <table>.<column>: <v1>; <v2>; . . . with 16 sampled values. Only the symbols final occurrence is pooled, and no synonyms are used anywhere. Common-KG, MultiFarm, Bio-ML, Anatomy: all symbols of both systems. df(f ) counts symbols, not tokens or views. String baselines. For formal statements and PubChem the Strings column is the best of word TFIDF, character 35-gram TF-IDF and BM25 over the statements: BM25 on Isabelle (0.825; word TF-IDF 0.772), word TF-IDF on Metamath (0.615; BM25 0.187) and character n-grams on HOL Light (0.741; word TF-IDF 0.669). Compute. One 48 GB A6000 (or two 24 GB A5000s with the model split across them) runs Gemma-2-9B plus the 131k SAE encoder (131,0723,584 in bfloat16, about 0.9 GB); Llama3.1-8B ran on one 40 GB A100 and Gemma-227B on two. sections.title: F XLCoST without the free hit
sections.content: The official XLCoST pool contains the querys own row, which every method retrieves first. Table 11 removes it, so the metrics count only the otherlanguage versions of each program. The ordering of the methods does not change: word TF-IDF is marginally ahead on MRR in five languages (by 0.0050.011) and SAE-IDF on Python and PHP, and SAE-IDF beats Dense in every language on both metrics, by up to +0.075 on precision at six (Java, 0.534 vs. 0.459).

sections.title: G Generated contexts
sections.content: Native views are the default throughout the paper. Table 12 instead describes each symbol with text that an LLM generates from its own systems data, either with one generator for both systems or with different generator for each, so that the two sides cannot share phrasing. Generated text raises every model-based method on MultiFarm (Dense from 0.650 to 0.780 on Chinese with two generators), and DensePC1 then matches or beats SAE-IDF: 0.825 vs. 0.819 on Chinese and 0.840 vs. 0.811 on Russian. generator can also add shared text that the systems themselves do not contain, as the drug-name run with shared metadata shows (Appendix M); the main table therefore uses native context only, which needs no generator.

Figure 5 repeats the layer and width sweeps on Common-KG and MultiFarm with the same SAE files (the 262k and matched-sparsity 16k/1M files were not available on the cluster used for these runs). Every evaluator also scores the alternatives to collection idf that the pipeline computes: an idf from Neuronpedias Pile activation densities (which needs no matched collection), an information weighting (log of in-symbol over background firing rate) and log-odds weighting. Collection idf is best on 10 of 13 comparisons  (Table 15)  ; the information weighting is close on ontology terms and tables, and the Pile-density idf is far behind on formal mathematics (0.190 vs. 0.661 on Metamath), where the generic features are specific to the pair of systems rather than to the Pile. Four-prover merge. Running all twelve ordered pairs among Lean 4, Isabelle, Metamath and HOL Light (Gemma-2-9B, layer 20) and merging mutual-top-1 matches into connected components gives Table 4: SAE-IDFs alignments are more precise and cover almost twice as many statements as dense at equal or higher consistency, so they merge into fewer components, closer to the 489 true problems. Transitivity is computed on the chained triples method links, so each method is measured on its own subset; DensePC1 removes the mean and first principal direction of all merged statements. The same procedure on XLCoST (911 programs in up to seven languages), where notations share their surface, gives transitivity 0.9987 for SAE-IDF and 0.9967 for dense and an adjusted Rand index of 0.983 and 0.962 (DensePC1 was not rerun there). Second model family on the main table. Table 1 includes Llama-3.1-8B with the Llama Scope layer-15 131k SAE on every main-table task with the same native views. SAE-IDF beats dense on 13 of the 14 rows and DensePC1 on 10: the formalmathematics gains carry over (Llamas dense state is far stronger on Metamath), Valentine improves (F1 0.625 vs. 0.588 dense, MRR 0.862), the knowledge-graph, cross-lingual and biomedical tasks are ties or small deficits against DensePC1 (NELL DBpedia 0.958 vs. 0.960, MultiFarm ru en 0.726 vs. 0.751, Anatomy 0.844 vs. 0.871), and on XLCoST SAE-IDF trails dense by 0.01 MRR while leading on Precision@6. Without the idf factor the Llama code stays below SAE-IDF on 13 of the 14 rows (all but XLCoST MRR, 0.448 vs. 0.442), and on the Bio-ML training split SAE-IDF reaches 0.789 against 0.727 for dense. Llama layers on knowledge-graph and crosslingual terms. Table 16 repeats the Common-KG and MultiFarm runs with every Llama Scope layer: the layer-15 ties with DensePC1 become leads at layers 8 and 12 on both knowledge-graph pairs; on MultiFarm (mean of the three language pairs) SAE-IDF leads at layers 12, 20 and 24 and trails DensePC1 by at most 0.012 at the others. Across the 18 (task, layer) cells SAE-IDF beats dense in 16 and DensePC1 in 10. Seed study. The only stochastic step is the sampling of views: up to 16 instances per CommonKG class and 16 cell values per Valentine column. Table 17 repeats the main-table runs with other sampling seeds (four seeds for Common-KG, three for Valentine); the ranges are far smaller than the gaps between methods. Feature-level decomposition and case studies Cases were selected per task by three rules, applied to the evaluations own rankings: wins, correct SAE-IDF matches whose gold counterpart Dense ranks 5th or worse, taking the shortest query texts with the widest SAE-IDF margin over the runnerup; failures, pairs where Dense ranks the gold counterpart first and SAE-IDF does not, taking the shortest; and the features with the largest SAE-IDF contributions over all decomposed matches of the task. For each case we list the golds rank under every method, the top five shared features with their share of the cosine and Pile density, the same pairs top shared features without weighting, and, for failures, the features shared with the wrong top candidate. One XLCoST failure is spurious, because the dataset contains the program twice. The full listings for the ten decomposed tasks (38 cases: 28 wins and 10 failures) are released with the code.

Every gain over Dense has < 0.004. The gain over DensePC1 has < 0.01 on every row except the three MultiFarm pairs and NELL DBpedia, where the interval covers zero. Against strings, SAE-IDF is significantly ahead on all formal-mathematics, knowledge-graph and ontology tasks (Lean 4 Metamath marginally, = 0.02), tied on XLCoST Python, PHP and C, and significantly behind word TF-IDF on XLCoST Java, C++, C# and JavaScript.
